title: De Trinitate libri duodecim
author: Hilary

passages.original: Hoc diserte do- cent Justinus martyr, Irenaeus, Origenes, Theophi- lus Antioch., Clemens Alexandr., Tertullianus, Cy- prianus, Patres Antiocheni concilii contra Paulum Samosat., ut mittamus Faustinum Presbyterum, Am- brosium, Leonem, aliosque plurimos. Sed ne ab iis quidem hoc negatum est, qui Ario favebant. Idipsum passim praedicat Eusebius in lib. Dem. Ev., et Sir- miense concilium contra Photinum eos anathemate damnat qui aliter senserint.
passages.english: This is expressly taught by Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Cyprian, and the Fathers of the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, to pass over Faustinus the Presbyter, Ambrose, Leo, and very many others. Indeed, not even those who favoured Arius denied this. Eusebius proclaims this very thing throughout his books of the Demonstration of the Gospel, and the Council of Sirmium against Photinus condemns with anathema those who think otherwise.
passages.notes: 'lib. Dem. Ev.' read as Eusebius' Demonstratio Evangelica.

passages.original: Sed cum in hoc doctrina fraudem moliti sint Ariani, ut Filium, qui visibilis ac visus sit, a Patre invisibili natura dissimilem praedicarent; alte retinendum, sanctos Patres ita Deum visum asseruisse, ut cum Augustino lib.iicontra Maximinum, cap. 26, n. 12, senserint, divinitatem non per substantiam suam, in qua invisibilis et immutabilis est, sed per creaturam sibi subjectam mortalium oculis appa- ruisse cum voluit. Ac ne peregrina huc adsciscamus, locuples hujus rei testis est Hilarius, lib.xii, n. 45 et 46. Certe, inquit, qui ante angelus, nunc etiam homo est : ne naturalem hanc esse Dei speciem diversitas hujus ipsius assumptae creationis pate- retur intelligi.
passages.english: But since the Arians contrived a deceit in this doctrine, so as to proclaim that the Son, who is visible and was seen, is unlike in nature to the invisible Father, it must be firmly held that the holy Fathers asserted that God was seen in such a way that they thought, with Augustine (book II against Maximinus, chapter 26, n. 12), that the divinity appeared to the eyes of mortals when it willed, not through its own substance, in which it is invisible and unchangeable, but through a creature subject to it. And, so as not to bring in foreign [witnesses] here, Hilary is an ample witness of this matter, book XII, n. 45 and 46: "Certainly," he says, "he who was before an angel is now also a man, so that the very diversity of this assumed created form would not allow this to be understood as the natural appearance of God."
passages.notes: 'lib.ii' read as book II (scanning run-together). The quotation from Hilary appears to continue into the following context.

passages.original: Non enim existimant angelos illos Dei ac Domini nomen sibi attribuisse, quia ut legati Dei ac Domini nomine loquebantur; quis enim legatus regis, impe- ratoris, aut principis sibi arroget nomen, cujus per- sonam repraesentat? sed ideo potius, quod Deus ipse in illis loquebatur. 71Hoc diserte docet Athanasius Or.ivcont. Arian., pag. 467: Is quidem, qui sentieba- tur oculis, angelus erat, sed Deus in angelo loque- batur. Nam quemadmodum in columna nubis verba ad Moysen in tabernaculo faciebat, ita quoque in angelis apparebat loquens Deus.
passages.english: For they do not think that those angels attributed to themselves the name of God and Lord because, as ambassadors, they spoke in the name of God and Lord (for what ambassador of a king, emperor, or prince would claim for himself the name of the one whose person he represents?), but rather because God himself spoke in them. Athanasius expressly teaches this, Oration IV against the Arians, p. 467: "He who was perceived by the eyes was indeed an angel, but God spoke in the angel. For just as he addressed words to Moses in the tabernacle in the pillar of cloud, so too God appeared speaking in angels."
passages.notes: The '71' before 'Hoc' is a page or column number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: 6. Ut Sabellius et Arius secum pugnantes rem agant Ecclesi. Compinge hujus (Sabellii) furori prsen- tium hreticorum (Arianorum) furorem, ut adversum Sabellium sibi adsint. Legisse se asserent, Pater ma- jor me est (Joan.
passages.english: 6. That Sabellius and Arius, fighting against each other, do the Church's business. Set against this madness (of Sabellius) the madness of the present heretics (the Arians), so that they may take each other's side against Sabellius. They will assert that they have read, "The Father is greater than I" (John
passages.notes: Scanning errors with lost ligatures (Ecclesi for Ecclesiae, prsentium for praesentium, hreticorum for haereticorum) are read as intended. "Ut adversum Sabellium sibi adsint" is difficult: the sense seems to be that the Arian madness is pitted against Sabellius so that the two errors confront one another. The heading and parenthetical glosses are the edition's. The citation continues in the following context (xiv, 28).

passages.original: 61, ex fide Ecclesiae, quae cum Christi naturas non confundat, nec dividat personas, in uno eodem- que Christo habet conquerentem ad mortem relic- tum se esse, quia homo est, et eum qui moritur profitentem se in paradiso regnare, quia Deus est. Interea Hilarius fidei necessitatem more suo commendat : quo arrogantiam retundat haereticorum, 321-322qui Christi mysteria se comprehendere jactitabant. Ut enim tradit Athanasius ad calcem l. de Salutari Adv. J. C. qui divinitati ejus passionem adscribunt, aut qui humanitati ejus fidem non ha- bent, aut qui unum in duo separant,ii carnis ejus dimensionem faciunt, et quantum et quomodo praeter sacras Scripturas definiunt, (??).
passages.english: [n.] 61, from the faith of the Church, which, since it neither confuses the natures of Christ nor divides the persons, holds in one and the same Christ the one who complains that he has been abandoned to death, because he is man, and the one who, as he dies, declares that he reigns in paradise, because he is God. Meanwhile Hilary, in his usual manner, commends the necessity of faith, in order to beat down the arrogance of the heretics, who boasted that they comprehended the mysteries of Christ. For, as Athanasius relates at the end of the book On the Saving Coming of Jesus Christ, those who ascribe suffering to his divinity, or who do not have faith in his humanity, or who separate the one into two, these make a measurement of his flesh, and define how much and in what way, beyond the Sacred Scriptures, (??).
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing 'num.' from the context: the sense is 'he resolves their knot at number 61'. '321-322' is an edition page marker and has been omitted. The '(??)' at the end stands in the edition, apparently for a Greek quotation that was not reproduced. The construction of the final clause is uncertain. 'l. de Salutari Adv. J. C.' is read as Athanasius' work on the saving advent (coming) of Jesus Christ.
